```{python}

LetsPlot.setup_html(isolated_frame=True)
```


```{python}

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/byuidatascience/data4missing/master/data-raw/flights_missing/flights_missing.json"
response = requests.get(url)
df = pl.read_json(io.BytesIO(response.content))
```


## QUESTION 1

__Calculate the sample size (i.e. number of rows in the dataset) for each airport in each year__. What do you notice?

Each airport has about 12 rows per year, but a lot of airport-year combinations are missing their rows entirely. This tells us the dataset is incomplete. Not every airport reported data for every month of every year. The gaps are scatered across airports and years, so any analysis that goes off of balanced panels will be wrong without accounting for missing months first.

```{python}
q1 = (
    df
    .group_by(["airport_code", "year"])
    .agg(pl.len().alias("sample_size"))
    .sort(["airport_code", "year"])
)

print(q1)
```

## QUESTION 2

__Which airport has the worst delays?__ Describe the metric you chose, and why you chose it to determine the "worst" airport. Your answer should include a summary table that lists (for each airport) the total number of flights, total number of delayed flights, proportion of delayed flights, and average delay time in hours.

I chose proportion of delayed flights as the primary metric because it controls for airport size. A busy place like Chicago will have more  delayed flights than a smaller airport because it handles more traffic. Proportion makes the comparison more balanced. As a secondary check I also calculated the average delay time in hours per delayed flight. SFO (San Francisco) ranks worst in comparison of delayed flights, meaning more of its departures are delayed compared to every other airport in this dataset.

```{python}
cols_needed = ["num_of_flights_total", "num_of_delays_total", "minutes_delayed_total"]

df_q2 = df.with_columns(
    pl.col(c).cast(pl.Float64, strict=False) for c in cols_needed
)

df_q2 = df_q2.filter(
    pl.all_horizontal(
        (pl.col(c).is_not_null()) & (pl.col(c) >= 0)
        for c in cols_needed
    )
)

summary = (
    df_q2
    .group_by("airport_code")
    .agg([
        pl.col("num_of_flights_total").sum().alias("total_flights"),
        pl.col("num_of_delays_total").sum().alias("total_delayed"),
        pl.col("minutes_delayed_total").sum().alias("total_minutes_delayed"),
    ])
    .with_columns([
        (pl.col("total_delayed") / pl.col("total_flights")).alias("prop_delayed"),
        (pl.col("total_minutes_delayed") / pl.col("total_delayed") / 60).alias("avg_delay_hours"),
    ])
    .drop("total_minutes_delayed")
    .sort("prop_delayed", descending=True)
)

print(summary)
```

## QUESTION 3

__Create a barplot showing the proportion of all flights that are delayed at each airport. Describe what you learn from this graph.__

The barplot makes the ranking pretty clear: SFO has the most delayed flights, while Salt Lake City (SLC) has the lowest. The spread between the best and worst airports is roughly 10 percent separating SLC from SFO. Most airports cluster in the 20–25% range, meaning roughly one in five flights is delayed regardless of airport. This suggests industry-wide causes (weather, air traffic control) play a large role, with airport-specific factors adding additional delays at the top of the chart.

```{python}
(
    ggplot(summary, aes(x="airport_code", y="prop_delayed"))
    + geom_bar(stat="identity", fill="#2166ac")
    + scale_y_continuous(format=".0%")
    + labs(
        title="Proportion of Flights Delayed by Airport",
        subtitle="Based on all available years in the dataset",
        x="Airport Code",
        y="Proportion of Flights Delayed",
    )
    + theme(
        plot_title=element_text(size=14),
        axis_title=element_text(size=11),
    )
)
```
